intro: Sculptures occupied public space, murals spread across walls, and painted books organized information into smaller fields. Each was made for a different kind of encounter.
alt: A stone head, a red wall painting, an open tribute manuscript and a folding pictorial book viewed by Microsoft.

variants.name: Olmec sculpture
variants.look: The stone head has solid rounded cheeks and a deeply defined band around the helmet.
variants.history: Olmec communities of the Gulf Coast of present-day Mexico made colossal basalt heads during the first millennium BCE and earlier. The heads are commonly interpreted as portraits of rulers.
variants.when: Study the head when a large sculpture must have a strong profile from multiple angles.
variants.why: Wide volumes and deep changes of plane make facial features legible at monument scale.

variants.name: Teotihuacan mural
variants.look: The red field holds broad ornamental bands that stay readable across a large wall.
variants.history: Teotihuacan flourished in central Mexico in the first millennium CE. Painters ornamented public and residential buildings with murals, many surviving only as fragments.
variants.when: Study the relationship between a large pattern and the architectural surface that carries it.
variants.why: Bands help a design continue across a wall even when the viewer is moving.

variants.name: Aztec codex
variants.look: Pictures are grouped into rows across an open book, with each cluster easy to find again.
variants.history: Central Mexican manuscripts recorded histories, tribute and other knowledge. The Codex Mendoza is a painted record made after the Spanish conquest, bringing Indigenous and European forms of record together.
variants.when: Study how the picture organizes repeated quantities and categories for someone consulting a page.
variants.why: Images and their spatial grouping let readers scan a record and revisit individual entries.

source.label: University of Texas at San Antonio Libraries

variants.name: Mixtec codex
variants.look: On the folding pages, a colored pathway draws the eye between small figures and places.
variants.history: Mixtec manuscripts from present-day southern Mexico use pictorial systems to record lineages, histories and places. Some survive on folded animal hide.
variants.when: Study how a path can link people, places and events without locking the story into a rectangular grid.
variants.why: A route through the picture gives the reader a way to track a dense history as the book unfolds.

source.label: British Museum on Google Arts & Culture

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. She is a visiting museumgoer, visibly present in a corner of each frame. Artwork gets most of the visual space. Scene list in exact order: Olmec colossal stone head with distinct helmet band and powerful rounded cheeks shown in exhibit courtyard; Teotihuacan wall-painting fragment with red iron-rich ground and broad bands of painted feathers; Aztec-era painted manuscript facsimile open to a scene of tribute goods organized in separated rows; Mixtec folding deerskin book facsimile seen at a low oblique angle, vivid red route, richly dressed small figures and architecture, no readable writing. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
